1.pericope_label: Moreover he made an altar of brass, twenty cubits the length thereof, and twenty cubits the breadth thereof, and ten cubits the height thereof. Also he made a molten sea of ten cubits from brim to brim, round in compass, and five cubits the height thereof; and a line of thirty cubits did compass it round about. And under it was the similitude of oxen, which did compass it round about: ten in a cubit, compassing the sea round about. Two rows of oxen were cast, when it was cast. It stood upon twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, and three looking toward the west, and three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east: and the sea was set above upon them, and all their hinder parts were inward. And the thickness of it was an handbreadth, and the brim of it like the work of the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies; and it received and held three thousand baths. He made also ten lavers, and put five on the right hand, and five on the left, to wash in them: such things as they offered for the burnt offering they washed in them; but the sea was for the priests to wash in.

schools.summary: Ellicott refuses the whole emending approach, arguing that the rows round the basin may have carried both oxen and gourds, that Reuss's objection from their small size underrates ancient art, and that the suspicion belongs rather to the copyist of Kings, so that it is sheer dogmatism to call the oxen an absurd change; on the capacity he prefers the accident that drops the numeral from Kings. Delitzsch sides against him in a clause, ascribing both differences to orthographical errors in the Chronicle, and separately declines a proposed excision as needless since the expression is merely pleonastic.

Clarke takes the Kings reading of the ornament for the true one and shows how two pairs of Hebrew letters could be confused to turn grapes into oxen, disposes of Houbigant's attempt to make both texts right by giving the word an Arabic sense it does not bear, explains the difference in capacity historically by the smaller Babylonish bath and reports the Targum cutting the knot with dry measure against liquid, and states the use of the lavers and of the sea.

debates: Which history was copied wrong at the ornament under the brim, where Clarke and Delitzsch both make this text corrupt and would restore the gourds from Kings, while Ellicott holds that both features may have been present and that the fault, if any, is in Kings.
Whether the sea held two thousand baths or three, where Clarke solves it by a smaller post-exilic measure and Ellicott by a numeral dropped from Kings, Delitzsch again putting it down to orthography.
Whether a verb in the fifth verse is a gloss imported from Kings, which Delitzsch denies on the ground that the expression is merely pleonastic.
outliers: Clarke traces Houbigant's error to a lexicon entry glossing ox-eye as a large black grape used in Palestine for a plum, and concludes that the criticism of this great man is not solid.
Ellicott meets the objection that oxen ten to the cubit would be too small by pointing to the reliefs on the bronze doors of Shalmaneser.

7.pericope_label: And he made ten candlesticks of gold according to their form, and set them in the temple, five on the right hand, and five on the left. He made also ten tables, and placed them in the temple, five on the right side, and five on the left. And he made an hundred basons of gold. Furthermore he made the court of the priests, and the great court, and doors for the court, and overlaid the doors of them with brass. And he set the sea on the right side of the east end, over against the south.

schools.summary: Delitzsch opens on the structural oddity that these verses are absent from the parallel narrative, can give no reason for the omission and concludes they must have dropped out, notes that neither court is further described, and twice rules out a named critic's reading of the furniture, denying that the tables were to bear the candlesticks and that the golden basons were for sprinkling blood. Ellicott makes the same structural point from the other side, renders the form of the candlesticks as their prescribed manner, corrects their position to before the chancel, supplies the philology of the late word for the outer court and the measurements of the bronze-plated doors at Balawat, and reads the position of the sea literally as the right shoulder eastward.

Clarke identifies the two courts as inner and outer, the latter the place where the people assembled, and calls the hundred basons a sort of sacrificial spoons for libations; Wesley glosses the form of the candlesticks as the old form God prescribed to Moses, and takes the ten tables for the shewbread, perhaps twelve loaves to each, the provision enlarged as the house was enlarged.

debates: What the ten tables were for, where Ellicott suggests the candelabra stood upon them and Delitzsch denies precisely that, holding with Wesley that they were for the shewbread.

What the hundred golden basons were, where Clarke, Ellicott and Delitzsch agree on vessels for libations and Delitzsch expressly rejects the reading that makes them vessels for catching and sprinkling blood.
What the phrase according to their form means, where Ellicott and Wesley agree on the prescribed manner and Ellicott sets aside the explanation that it means as their use required.
outliers: Ellicott supplies a measure from excavation for the bronze plating of the doors, the leaves at Balawat standing twenty-two feet high and six feet wide.
themes: And he made ten candlesticks of gold according to their form, and set them in the temple, five on the right hand, and five on the left.

11.pericope_label: And Huram made the pots, and the shovels, and the basons. And Huram finished the work that he was to make for king Solomon for the house of God; To wit, the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars; And four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath, to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were upon the pillars. He made also bases, and lavers made he upon the bases; One sea, and twelve oxen under it. The pots also, and the shovels, and the fleshhooks, and all their instruments, did Huram his father make to king Solomon for the house of the Lord of bright brass. In the plain of Jordan did the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredathah. Thus Solomon made all these vessels in great abundance: for the weight of the brass could not be found out.

schools.summary: Ellicott works the list for text and translation, judging pots right against the lavers of Kings on the strength of a single stroke, finding the repeated verb at the bases a corruption of the numeral ten and ancient enough to show in the Greek, preferring globes and capitals to pommels and chapiters and settling what the numeral counts by the gender of the words, reading the wreaths as lattices, weighing whether fleshhooks or bowls belongs in the catalogue, rejecting the idea that the instruments were the moulds since moulds are not of polished brass, and recording that the Syriac and Arabic omit the whole stretch. Delitzsch places the half verse about the copper utensils with what precedes rather than with the catalogue that follows.

Clarke makes the title a term of office, the Hebrew word being used of a master or chief operator, and reports that some suppose the vessels were not cast at the sites named but that the clay was carried from that quarter as the most proper for moulds; Wesley makes the same title one of respect for the craftsman's art and service.

Henry supplies the provenance of the title Father Huram from the Tyrian king's own usage, and draws two observations from the summary, that the workman was punctual and left no part of his work undone and that the king was generous, making many vessels of a sort so that many hands might be employed and some be laid up against the wearing out of others, the surplus brass being devoted to God and not to be turned to his own use.

debates: What it means to call the craftsman Huram his father: a term of office for a master or chief operator (Clarke), a title of respect for his art (Wesley), or a nickname taken over from the Tyrian king's own words (Henry).
Whether the instruments of the sixteenth verse are fleshhooks or bowls, where Ellicott prefers bowls but allows that both words may belong since the law names all four utensils in succession.

Whether those instruments could be the moulds the vessels were cast in, which Ellicott denies because moulds would not be of polished brass, while Clarke reports the related view that only the clay was carried from the named sites.
outliers: Ellicott finds the repeated verb at the bases to be a corruption of the numeral ten, which closely resembles it in Hebrew writing, and shows the error to be ancient because the Greek reproduces it.
Ellicott records that the Syriac and Arabic omit this whole stretch of the chapter, which bears on the weight of those versions wherever they are cited elsewhere in it.

19.pericope_label: And Solomon made all the vessels that were for the house of God, the golden altar also, and the tables whereon the shewbread was set; Moreover the candlesticks with their lamps, that they should burn after the manner before the oracle, of pure gold; And the flowers, and the lamps, and the tongs, made he of gold, and that perfect gold; And the snuffers, and the basons, and the spoons, and the censers, of pure gold: and the entry of the house, the inner doors thereof for the most holy place, and the doors of the house of the temple, were of gold.

schools.summary: Ellicott charges the writer with an inconsistency he cannot resolve, speaking of tables in the plural here and twice elsewhere where Kings has one only, yet elsewhere again of a single Pure Table, and guesses that a number of tables found in one source were grouped with the table of shewbread, gaining brevity at the cost of accuracy; on the phrase for perfect gold he settles the derivation against Bishop Wordsworth and defends the clause as characteristic of the writer against a critic who suspects it. Delitzsch registers the same divergence more mildly, explains why the number and position of the candlesticks are omitted here, agrees that the rare phrase is genuine though it looks superfluous, and does the inventory work on the knives and the forks.

Clarke pictures each branch of the chandelier as a plant in flower whose opening was the lamp or its support, and closes the chapter with a protest about method, granting that everything in the tabernacle and temple was typical of some excellence of the Gospel but refusing the detailed application of knops and flowers and tongs to particular doctrines as weak, silly, religious trifling; Wesley glosses the rule for the lamps as the prescription God gave to Moses.

debates: Whether the plural tables of shewbread can be reconciled with this writer's own singular elsewhere, which Ellicott says cannot be settled with certainty and explains as brevity at the cost of accuracy.
Whether the clause rendered that perfect gold is genuine, which the Greek omits and a critic suspects, and which both Ellicott and Delitzsch defend.
From which of two similar verbs the rare word for perfection derives, where Ellicott decides against Bishop Wordsworth.
outliers: Clarke protests against the detailed typological reading of the furniture, naming the author of Solomon's Temple Spiritualized, and holds such spiritualizing ill calculated to produce respect for divine revelation.
themes: And Solomon made all the vessels that were for the house of God, the golden altar also, and the tables whereon the shewbread was set;
Moreover the candlesticks with their lamps, that they should burn after the manner before the oracle, of pure gold;
